summary:
2 Chronicles continues 1 Chronicles without a break — the two were a single book in Hebrew tradition — and runs from Solomon's accession to the fall of Jerusalem, ending two verses beyond it. Solomon asks God for "wisdom and knowledge" to govern (1:10), and the first nine chapters center on the temple: its construction on the threshing floor David bought (3:1), and a dedication at which fire comes down from heaven and the glory of the LORD so fills the house that the priests cannot enter (7:1–2). In a night vision God then gives Solomon the sentence the rest of the book keeps testing, a line still widely quoted: "if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land" (7:14).

After Solomon the kingdom splits (chapter 10), and Chronicles stays with Judah and the line of David; the breakaway northern kingdom's rulers enter the story only as they affect Judah. The reforming kings get the space: Asa and Jehoshaphat tear down foreign altars; Hezekiah reopens the neglected temple and holds a great Passover — kept a month late so priests and people can prepare — inviting even survivors of the fallen northern tribes (30); Josiah's temple renovation turns up the lost Book of the Law (34). The starkest turnaround is Manasseh, whose fifty-five-year reign is Judah's longest: taken to Babylon in shackles by the Assyrians, he "humbled himself before the God of his fathers," is restored, and clears out the idols (33:11–15) — a repentance the parallel account in 2 Kings 21 does not mention. Reign by reign the vocabulary of 7:14 recurs: kings seek God or forsake Him, humble themselves or refuse.

The last kings do not turn: "they mocked the messengers of God… until the wrath of the LORD against His people was stirred up beyond remedy" (36:16). Babylon burns the temple and carries Judah into exile, and the book gives the catastrophe a prophetic timetable: the land "enjoyed its Sabbath rest" until seventy years were completed, "in fulfillment of the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah" (36:21; Jeremiah 25:11; 29:10). Then the final two verses leap to 538 BC: Cyrus king of Persia, whose empire had swallowed Babylon the year before, proclaims that the exiles may go home and rebuild — "Whoever among you belongs to His people, may the LORD his God be with him, and may he go up" (36:23). Ezra 1 opens with this same decree, and in the traditional Hebrew ordering of the Scriptures Chronicles stands last — which makes Cyrus's summons to go up and rebuild the Hebrew Bible's closing sentence.
